column2: The no-king setting introduces a Levite in Ephraim's remote hill country and his taking a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
column3: Remote parts renders the geographical thighs/flanks idiom; woman-concubine is represented by the established English status term.

column2: The selected account says she became angry with him, left for her father's Bethlehem house and stayed four months; no allegation of sexual unfaithfulness is inserted.
He follows to speak to her heart, reconcile her to himself and bring her back; all three purposes remain with the servant, two animals and father's welcome.
The young woman's father receives his son-in-law, and the three-day stay includes eating, drinking and sleeping; the contextual in-law relationship resolves gambros here.
Fourth-day early rising leads to the father's heart-strengthening bread invitation and plural go command; ordinary English go does not display the selected plural.
Both men eat and drink together; begin by lodging preserves the unusual arxamenos before the invitation to a glad heart.
column3: The exact force of arxamenos is unresolved, and this night is the temporal sense of lodging in context rather than a separately expressed noun.

column2: The man rises to leave but is pressed by his father-in-law and stays again; again is explicitly supported by palin.
Fifth-day morning departure is delayed by bread and remaining until day declines; both men again eat and drink in the narrated sequence.
column3: Remain for strateuomai interprets the unusual verb as staying/camping here; its lexical force needs review and is not silently treated as ordinary meno.

column2: The father addresses the departing party with behold, another day's lodging, a glad heart and tomorrow's journey and dwelling; all invitations remain.
column3: May rise renders the future as permissive advice in the invitation; the Greek changes from plural rising and your journey to singular going and your dwelling.

column2: Refusal to lodge leads to departure toward Jebus, explicitly identified as Jerusalem, with saddled animals and concubine.
The late hour at Jebus prompts the servant's invitation to lodge in that Jebusite city; the master/servant relation is retained.
The master's emphatic refusal is singular, followed by collective we will pass on to Gibeah; the city is rejected as outside Israel.
He offers Gibeah or Ramah as lodging alternatives; neither destination is silently selected before the narrative does so.
Their onward movement is linked by for to sunset near Benjamin's Gibeah; the tribal location remains.
They enter Gibeah and sit in its square, with no host taking them in; the repeated lodging purpose remains.
Behold introduces the old man returning from field work; he sojourns from Ephraim while the locality's people are Benjaminites.
He lifts his eyes, sees the traveler and asks destination before origin; the question order remains.
The Levite names Bethlehem and remote Ephraim, says he returns to his own house and lacks a host; no house-of-the-Lord destination is substituted.
Fodder for their donkeys and bread/wine for himself, the woman and the young man support the claim of lacking nothing; respectful servant terms remain.
column3: Your servants gathers the party under the final plural address formula; it is not evidence that they are literally owned by the old man.

column2: Propose Still and but for the two plen transitions: the host assumes every need despite the traveler's supplies and forbids sleeping in the square.
column3: The change removes an exclusive only while retaining the host's reassurance and contrast; let all your need fall on me remains the source's burden image.

column2: The old man brings him in and feeds the animals, then they wash feet, eat and drink; the change from singular host action to plural guests is retained.
Propose behold to retain idou at the arrival of the lawless men's sons; surrounding, pounding the door and the demand to know the guest remain.
column3: Know is a sexual demand in this threatening context, not a request for acquaintance; restrained source idiom here is clarified by the explicit violence in verse 25.

column2: The householder appeals to his brothers not to act wickedly or commit folly because the man entered his house; this is the speaker's rationale, not editorial endorsement.
The offer of the virgin daughter and concubine, violation, doing what is good in their eyes and protection of the male guest all remain as the householder's speech.
column3: Violate expresses the sexual humiliation intended by tapeinoo here; the narrator's report is not softened or expanded with a moralizing gloss.

column2: The men refuse to listen, the man seizes and expels his concubine, and the attackers rape and mock her all night until releasing her at dawn.
column3: Raped renders knew in the coercive context; responsibility for handing her over remains with the man, without passive wording that conceals his agency.

column2: She reaches and falls at the gateway of the house where her master is, remaining until daylight; her movement and location remain.
Her master prepares to leave, then behold introduces her fallen body with hands at the threshold; neither the threshold detail nor the presentative is omitted.
Propose but she had died to preserve alla's contrast with the absent response; the selected text explicitly states death before lifting her onto the animal.
column3: The wording is not harmonized to witnesses lacking the death statement; the adversative remains English even though death also explains her silence.

column2: At home he takes the knife and divides her according to her bones into twelve portions, sent to all Israel's tribes; the actions and number remain explicit without invented anatomical detail.
The witnesses' unprecedented-since-Egypt statement and the sender's full instruction both remain; the repeated time span and counsel about her conclude the selected longer unit.
